prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks (B005) to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full exchange I hold it with somewhat more confidence, because the chair's summary shows that the opposing case, B014, has the same structure of strengths and weaknesses as mine but with a shorter record. The decisive scientific step in B005 is a single, falsifiable idea: trap many atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and thereby trade the single-ion statistics limit for parallel interrogation of a large ensemble. The realization at about 1e-18, reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories and species on three continents, shows the idea was right and was not a one-group artefact. Every member who proposes names for this ballot proposes exactly Katori and Ye, so the credit question is as settled as anything on this shortlist can be. Following the chair's question on citation, I would keep the wording narrow and tied to the invention, magic-wavelength trapping and the accuracy reached, and not to precision timekeeping in general, ultrastable lasers or the not-yet-realized redefinition of the second. On Ye's role, my reading of the round-1 record is that the citation should say 'invention and realization' jointly: Katori conceived the scheme and led the first lattice spectroscopy, Ye took it to record accuracy and into the many-body regime. I flag that this division rests on recollection and on the colleagues' statements, not on the primary papers, which the committee should check before the vote.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains subject overlap. The 2005 prize (frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including Wineland's optical ion clocks) sit next to this territory, and a committee wanting a result where nature surprised us, in the sense of my remark that physicists must find clues in nature, could regard a lattice clock as a superb instrument and not a discovery. Second, the payoff through the redefinition of the second is prospective. Third, two names leave out other strontium and ytterbium lattice-clock groups (Paris, PTB and others), ultrastable-laser developers and the competing ion-clock route, and I cannot settle fine priority between Tokyo and Boulder from the supplied material. I take these seriously. They do not change my ranking because none of them breaks the credit: the overlap argument says the field has been honoured nearby, not that this invention has been, and the new element here is the many-atom lattice interrogation that the earlier prizes did not cover.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from KPZ to B014 and frames the choice as a new-phenomenon prize versus a measurement-science prize, asking whether a clock is a discovery about nature or an instrument achievement.
responses.response: That is the right criterion and I will answer it directly. The lattice clock is an invention, but it is not only an instrument: reaching 1e-18 opened a quantitative window on many-body physics in the lattice, on relativistic geodesy and on bounds on drifting constants, which are statements about nature. Still, I concede that B014 produced something nature had not been known to contain, and I do not claim B005 is the more surprising of the two. My ranking turns on a different criterion: for a prize the committee must be able to defend both the claim and the credit years from now. B014 asks us to defend a 2018 result whose mechanism is unresolved, with a lead author and earlier band-structure theorists outside the trio. I would put that choice to the committee as a judgment about robustness, not as a verdict that instruments cannot be discoveries.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B014 is a rare clean theory-to-experiment line, that confirmation is strong even with the pairing mechanism open, and that waiting will not improve the case.
responses.response: I accept the first two points and I moved my own B014 estimate upward because of your argument that the correlated insulators and superconducting dome were reproduced within months. Where I differ is the last point. If waiting would not improve the case, it also would not harm it, whereas the attribution problem for B014 is not about time: Yuan Cao, Cory Dean's group and the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto band-structure work are all outside a three-seat list, and you yourself say the 2011 priority question has not been checked against sources. I would be content to see B014 prevail if the committee verifies the 2011 priority and decides a MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer trio is defensible, but on the evidence in this room B005 is the safer single prize this year.

responses.point: Lindroth, an atomic theorist, says the magic-wavelength proposal and first realization are Katori's, that Ye brought the clock to record accuracy and into the many-body regime, and that a two-name split is coherent.
responses.response: Thank you; this answers the question I put to you in round 1 well enough for me to settle the wording. I read Ye's part as a decisive realization that also extended the idea, so I now propose the citation 'invention and realization' with magic-wavelength trapping named explicitly, which credits Katori for the concept and both for the realization. I do add one caution that you flagged yourself: your proximity to the field may lead you to read the ion-clock competition as less decisive than it is. I have no independent basis to rank Al+ ion clocks below lattice clocks, only that the 2012 prize covered the ion route and the lattice route is the many-atom step.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B005 first, emphasizes the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and records the third-prize-in-a-neighbouring-territory reservation together with the outside precision-laser connection through Hall's laboratory in Boulder.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and I share your third reservation, which I think is the most serious against B005. I would add one thing to your disclosure: since your doctoral stay was in Hall's laboratory, the committee should treat your confident reading of Boulder's role, and of Ye's share in particular, with a little extra care, and verify priority from papers and not from familiarity. That said, I do not think the stay changes the conclusion, because the Katori and Ye split does not depend on Hall.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks the committee to say clearly whether an incomplete trio is acceptable for B055 and notes the lattice clock is not exposed to that problem.
responses.response: I take your question as the reason I keep B055 only as an alternative. My view is that an incomplete trio is acceptable only when the omission can be defended on the scientific record, and for ATLAS and CMS I cannot defend a cut among Gianotti, Evans, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, so I would not advance it this year. I also agree with your caution in round 1 that a citation for B005 should not blur lattice clocks into ion clocks, which is why my citation names magic-wavelength trapping and a specific accuracy and not precision timekeeping generally.

responses.point: Olsson says B005 has the most compact attribution, with a conceptual originator and a performance leader, but also notes that B014 has a wider effect on condensed-matter physics and may outrank a measurement-science advance.
responses.response: I agree with the compact attribution and I think your last sentence is the honest centre of this committee's disagreement. The wider reach of B014 is real, and if the committee ranks breadth of influence above record and credit, B014 should win. I would only add that B005 has its own breadth, because lattice clocks now serve geodesy, constants tests and many-body physics, so the difference is smaller than the framing 'one field versus many' suggests. I would not resist B014 if the committee prefers it, which is why it is my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges a third precision-measurement prize (after 2005 and 2012) a distinct achievement or an incremental refinement. This is my largest single reservation and a stricter reading could reverse the order of B005 and B014.

Whether Ye's role is best worded as co-invention or as record-accuracy realization. I propose 'invention and realization', but the Tokyo versus Boulder priority record is from memory and should be checked against the primary papers.

Whether B014 would, after verification of the 2011 priority question and of Yuan Cao's and Cory Dean's roles, offer a defensible three-name list. I remain close to indifferent between B005 and B014 on science and prefer B005 on record and credit only.

How much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry. I treat it as an unrealized application that does not affect the validity of the invention, but another member could reasonably treat it as a maturity concern.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile for B005 (Katori, Ye) or for B014 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer). My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, early mentor Hector Rubinstein, co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is among the credited names. My two years at CERN after the PhD is a general institutional link to B055, which is only an alternative, and my profile records no tie to any of its named individuals. My field is high-energy theory and cosmology, so I am not a specialist judge of atomic precision measurement or of moiré condensed matter and I rely on colleagues' technical statements.
